drills.title: Deferred revenue jumps while revenue looks flat
drills.scenario: An AI SaaS company moves customers from monthly to annual prepaid contracts. Reported revenue grows 8% year over year, but operating cash flow grows 45% and deferred revenue on the balance sheet nearly doubles (illustrative).
drills.question: Is the business slowing down or speeding up, and which line tells you?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Probably speeding up. Under ASC 606 cash collected up front sits in deferred revenue and is recognized ratably, so annual billing pulls cash forward without lifting revenue yet. Look at billings (revenue plus the change in deferred revenue) and remaining performance obligations. If billings grew far faster than revenue, bookings are healthy and revenue will follow over the contract terms.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Reading flat revenue as flat demand, or the reverse: treating a one-time billing-term switch as permanent growth. Strip out the switch and compare like-for-like billings.

drills.title: Profitable on paper, out of cash in six months
drills.scenario: A robotics startup reports its first profitable year: $4M of net income on $30M revenue. Receivables rose $6M, inventory rose $5M and it bought $3M of equipment (illustrative). The bank balance fell.
drills.question: Reconcile profit to cash in under a minute and name the fix.
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Operating cash flow is roughly 4 + depreciation - 6 (AR) - 5 (inventory), so about -$6M before depreciation, and free cash flow is about -$9M after the $3M of capex. Growth is being funded through working capital. Fixes: tighten payment terms or deposits, cut days of inventory, and line up a working capital facility before the cash runs out, not after.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Celebrating net income while ignoring the cash conversion cycle. Many growing hardware companies fail profitable.

drills.title: The GPU useful-life lever
drills.scenario: A cloud provider extends the useful life of its servers from 4 to 6 years. Operating income rises by several billion dollars the next year with no change in customer demand (illustrative magnitude).
drills.question: What happened economically, and what should an investor or board ask?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Nothing changed in cash: capex is the same, only the depreciation schedule moved. Annual depreciation on a given fleet falls by about a third (1/4 to 1/6 per year), so margins rise mechanically. Ask whether real refresh cycles support 6 years, especially for AI accelerators whose economic life may be shorter than the accounting life, and compare capex to depreciation over time.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Crediting management with margin expansion that is purely an estimate change. The reverse trap is ignoring a future impairment if the hardware becomes obsolete early.

drills.title: Goodwill write-down after a marquee deal
drills.scenario: HP bought Autonomy in 2011 for about $11B and in November 2012 wrote down about $8.8B, attributing more than $5B of it to alleged accounting improprieties at the target (public record).
drills.question: What does an impairment of this size tell you about the original deal, and what should a board check before the next acquisition?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Goodwill is the premium over identifiable net assets, so a write-down of most of the price says the cash flows assumed at signing are not there. Before the next deal: independent quality-of-earnings work on revenue recognition (especially hardware or reseller revenue booked as software), a walk-away price set before the auction heats up, and integration milestones tied to the synergy case.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Treating impairment as a non-cash, ignore-it item. The cash was spent at closing; the write-down is just the admission.

drills.title: Adjusted EBITDA that excludes the business
drills.scenario: An AI startup's investor deck shows positive adjusted EBITDA. The add-backs include stock-based compensation equal to 25% of revenue, 'one-time' GPU training runs that recur every quarter, and capitalized software development (illustrative).
drills.question: Which add-backs would you reverse, and what number would you use instead?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Reverse SBC (it is a real cost paid in dilution), reverse recurring training spend (if it happens every quarter it is operating cost), and look through capitalized development by using free cash flow after capitalized software. A cleaner view is free cash flow minus SBC per diluted share. If that is deeply negative, the business is not near breakeven.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Accepting management's non-GAAP definitions because they are common in the sector. Every add-back needs a reason it will not recur.

drills.title: Read a tech 10-K in 15 minutes
drills.scenario: You have 15 minutes before a meeting with a public software company you have never studied. You have its latest 10-K open.
drills.question: In what order do you read it, and what three numbers do you write down?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Business section and risk factors for the model and the biggest stated risks, then MD&A for the drivers management itself highlights, then the cash flow statement before the income statement, then revenue recognition and segment notes. Write down revenue growth, free cash flow margin after SBC, and remaining performance obligations or deferred revenue growth. Finish with share count trend to catch dilution.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Starting with the income statement and the adjusted numbers in the press release. The footnotes and cash flow statement are where the quality shows.

drills.title: Breakeven at the pub
drills.scenario: A pub sells beer at $3.50 with a variable cost of $2.30 per beer (Foster ACCTG 501 class problem figures). Monthly fixed costs are $6,000 (illustrative).
drills.question: How many beers a month to break even, and what happens if you cut the price to $3.20?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Contribution margin is $1.20, so breakeven is 6,000 / 1.20 = 5,000 beers. At $3.20 the margin drops to $0.90 and breakeven rises to about 6,667 beers, a 33% volume increase just to stand still. A 9% price cut needs a third more volume.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Cutting price for volume without computing the new breakeven. Thin-margin businesses need far more volume than intuition suggests.

drills.title: Build vs buy with the instructor's numbers
drills.scenario: In the HP buy-versus-build case (Foster ACCTG 501, Case 4.1 instructor solution), the present value of costs is about $13.01M to build and $10.62M to buy at a 7.5% discount rate. A team draft in the course folder had recommended building.
drills.question: What is the decision, and how did the team get the opposite answer?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Buy: building has an incremental NPV of roughly -$2.39M. Opposite answers in build-vs-buy usually come from counting sunk costs, allocating existing fixed overhead to the buy option, or leaving out the build option's later maintenance and opportunity cost of engineers. Only future, differential cash flows count.
drills.antiPatternTrap: The engineer's bias to build because the team can. For AI models the same trap shows up as training in-house when an API or open model is cheaper over the horizon.

drills.title: ROI ranks one way, EVA ranks the other
drills.scenario: Three country divisions report ROI of 28.3%, 28.0% and 1.0%, and EVA of 174.5, 290.5 and -90.2 at a 20% cost of capital (Foster ACCTG 501 class problem figures, in thousands).
drills.question: Which division creates the most value, and why do the two measures disagree?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: The 28.0% division creates the most value: EVA of 290.5 beats 174.5 because it earns above the 20% hurdle on a larger capital base. ROI is a ratio and ignores scale. The 1.0% division destroys value and needs a fix-or-exit plan. Paying managers on ROI can make them reject projects that earn 25%, above the hurdle but below their current ROI.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Ranking divisions or products on percentage returns alone. Absolute value created above the cost of capital is what compounds.

drills.title: Transfer price standoff
drills.scenario: A components division sells to an internal assembly division at $220 a unit. The assembly division can buy the same part outside for $200. The components division has idle capacity and a variable cost of $190 (Foster ACCTG 501 class problem figures).
drills.question: What range of transfer prices is good for the company, and what happens if the seller holds at $220?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: With idle capacity, any price between $190 (seller's variable cost) and $200 (buyer's outside price) keeps the work inside and is good for the company. If the seller insists on $220, the buyer goes outside at $200 and the company is $10 a unit worse off, because it pays $200 cash instead of using $190 of internal variable cost.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Letting divisional P&L incentives override company-level contribution. Transfer prices should follow opportunity cost, not full cost plus a markup.

drills.title: Leverage raises the cost of equity, not firm value
drills.scenario: Hargrove has an asset beta of 4.53, a 5% risk-free rate and a 5% market risk premium, so its all-equity cost of capital is 27.65%. It recapitalizes to 33% debt with a debt beta of 0.38, in a world without taxes (Foster FIN 502 class problem figures).
drills.question: What is the new cost of equity, and did the recap create value?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Equity beta becomes (4.53 - 0.33 x 0.38) / 0.67, about 6.57, so the cost of equity is about 37.85%. Cost of debt is 5% + 5% x 0.38 = 6.9%. WACC is 0.67 x 37.85% + 0.33 x 6.9%, about 27.65%, unchanged. With no taxes or distress costs, Modigliani-Miller holds: cheaper debt is offset by riskier equity, and value does not move.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Saying debt is cheaper so borrowing lowers WACC. Value from leverage comes only from tax shields net of distress costs.

drills.title: The terminal value is 80% of the DCF
drills.scenario: An analyst values a software company with a 5-year DCF. Terminal value uses 4.5% perpetual growth at a 6% WACC and makes up 82% of enterprise value (illustrative).
drills.question: What is wrong, and how would you pressure-test it in three minutes?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: The Gordon multiple is 1/(WACC - g) = 1/1.5%, about 67x next year's cash flow, so tiny input changes swing value wildly. Perpetual growth should not exceed long-run nominal GDP growth, and WACC must stay well above g. Run a WACC-vs-g grid, cross-check the implied exit EV/FCF multiple against mature peers, and ask what the explicit forecast period needs to show for the value to hold.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Presenting a precise DCF value when most of it rests on two assumptions in the denominator.

drills.title: Growth that destroys value
drills.scenario: A business earns $100M of NOPAT with a 9% return on invested capital against a 10% WACC. The CEO proposes doubling reinvestment to grow faster (illustrative).
drills.question: Should the board fund faster growth?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Not yet. When ROIC is below WACC, every reinvested dollar earns less than investors require, so faster growth destroys value. First lift ROIC above WACC through pricing, mix or capital efficiency, then grow. Growth is only valuable when the spread ROIC minus WACC is positive.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Treating revenue growth as good by default. The spread decides whether growth helps or hurts.

drills.title: Buyback or reinvest
drills.scenario: A large-cap tech company has $20B of excess cash. Its shares trade at 30x free cash flow. Management proposes a $20B buyback while R&D budgets are being cut (illustrative).
drills.question: How would you frame the capital allocation decision for the board?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Rank uses by return versus cost of capital: high-return internal projects first, then acquisitions with a clear edge, then debt paydown, then return cash. A buyback at 30x FCF earns about a 3.3% FCF yield, so it only beats reinvestment if internal projects earn less than that or the stock is undervalued on a sober intrinsic value. Cutting R&D to fund a buyback trades long-term moat for short-term EPS.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Doing buybacks to hit EPS targets or offset SBC dilution without asking whether the price is below intrinsic value.

drills.title: VC method backsolve
drills.scenario: A seed investor targets a 10x return. The startup could plausibly be worth $200M at exit in 7 years, and the investor expects 50% dilution from later rounds. The founders ask for $3M (illustrative).
drills.question: What post-money valuation can the investor accept?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Required ownership at exit is 3 x 10 / 200 = 15%. With 50% dilution, ownership today must be 15% / 0.5 = 30%. Post-money is then $3M / 30% = $10M, so pre-money is $7M. If founders want a higher price they must show a bigger exit or less future dilution.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Negotiating on today's headline valuation while ignoring the dilution path to exit.

drills.title: Burn multiple and the bridge round
drills.scenario: A Series A company burns $1.5M a month, adds $400k of net new ARR a month, and has 9 months of cash (illustrative).
drills.question: Is it fundable, and what would you do this quarter?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Burn multiple is net burn / net new ARR = 1.5 / 0.4 = 3.75, which is poor; under about 2 is usually considered efficient. With 9 months of runway and a fundraise taking about 6, it needs to act now: cut burn to stretch runway past 18 months or show a falling burn multiple, and raise a bridge from insiders only if they see a credible path to efficiency.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Waiting until 3 months of runway to fundraise, which hands all negotiating power to investors.

drills.title: LTV/CAC that hides a cash problem
drills.scenario: A B2B AI startup shows LTV/CAC of 5x. CAC is $60k, monthly gross profit per customer is $2k, and annual churn is 8%, so LTV is about $24k / 0.08 = $300k (illustrative).
drills.question: Is 5x good news? What else must you check?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: The ratio is fine, but CAC payback is 60 / 2 = 30 months, so each new customer drains cash for 2.5 years. Fast growth will burn heavily even with good unit economics. Check payback (often targeted under 12 to 18 months for mid-market), whether LTV uses gross profit not revenue, and whether churn is measured on enough mature cohorts.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Quoting LTV/CAC alone. A great ratio with a long payback can still sink a startup that cannot fund the gap.

drills.title: The option pool shuffle
drills.scenario: A VC offers $10M on an $8M pre-money valuation, on condition that a 15% post-money option pool is created inside the pre-money (illustrative).
drills.question: What is the founders' effective pre-money valuation?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Post-money is $18M. The 15% pool is $2.7M of value carved out of the pre-money, so the founders' effective pre-money is $8M - $2.7M = $5.3M. Push back by sizing the pool to an actual 12-to-18-month hiring plan, or by putting part of it in the post-money.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Comparing term sheets on headline pre-money without adjusting for the pool.

drills.title: Full ratchet in a down round
drills.scenario: Series A investors bought preferred at $2.00 with full-ratchet anti-dilution. The company now raises at $1.60 (Foster ENTRE 542 VCIC term sheet example).
drills.question: What happens to the Series A, and how would you negotiate it?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Under full ratchet the Series A conversion price resets to $1.60, so each preferred share converts into 2.00 / 1.60 = 1.25 common shares, a 25% increase, with all the extra dilution falling on founders and employees. Broad-based weighted average would adjust far less. Negotiate for broad-based weighted average up front, or ask the Series A to waive the ratchet as a condition of the new round.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Ignoring anti-dilution terms in good times. They only bite in a down round, which is exactly when founders have least leverage.

drills.title: Power law math for a $150M fund
drills.scenario: A $150M venture fund (sized like the Foster ENTRE 542 VCIC simulation) wants to return 3x net, so about $450M back to LPs. Its typical ownership at exit is 10% (illustrative).
drills.question: What size of exit does the fund need, and what does that mean for which startups it backs?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: To return $450M from a single winner at 10% ownership it needs a $4.5B exit, and in practice one or two outliers produce most of the return. So the fund must back companies that could plausibly reach multi-billion outcomes, even if most fail. A great $100M business is a poor fit for this fund, no matter how healthy.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Founders pitching a solid niche business to a fund whose math needs outliers, then reading the rejection as a verdict on the business.

drills.title: Raise price 10%, lose 6% of volume
drills.scenario: A subscription app raises its monthly price from $10 to $11. Subscribers fall 6%. Variable cost per subscriber is $2 (illustrative).
drills.question: Was it a good move?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Demand is inelastic here (elasticity about -0.6). Revenue goes from 100 x 10 = 1,000 to 94 x 11 = 1,034 per 100 original subscribers, up 3.4%. Contribution goes from 100 x 8 = 800 to 94 x 9 = 846, up 5.75%. Good move, as long as the churn does not keep rising in later months.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Judging a price change on subscriber count alone, or measuring only the first month before delayed churn shows up.

drills.title: Why rate hikes crushed software multiples
drills.scenario: Between 2022 and mid-2023 the Federal Reserve raised its policy rate from near zero to above 5%. Many high-growth software stocks lost more than half their value even where revenue kept growing (public record, broad pattern).
drills.question: Explain the mechanism to a board in two sentences, and what it means for the startup's plan.
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Higher risk-free rates raise the discount rate, and long-duration assets whose cash flows sit far in the future lose the most value. For a startup this means investors reward near-term free cash flow over distant growth, so plans should show a credible path to breakeven and better burn multiples.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Blaming the drawdown on execution alone, or assuming valuations will snap back to zero-rate levels.

drills.title: Five forces on an AI model wrapper
drills.scenario: A startup sells a writing assistant built on a third-party foundation model API. Margins are 60% today. Two large model providers are launching similar features in their own apps.
drills.question: Run a fast five-forces check and state the main risk.
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Supplier power is high: the model provider sets price and can integrate forward. Buyer switching costs are low, rivalry is high, entry barriers are low, and substitutes include the providers' own apps. The main risk is margin squeeze plus forward integration. Durable defense needs proprietary data or workflow lock-in, deep integration into customer systems, or multi-model sourcing to cut supplier power.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Mistaking today's margin for a moat. Margins on rented capability belong to whoever controls the scarce input.

drills.title: Which of the 7 Powers is real?
drills.scenario: A founder claims their AI startup has 'a data moat, network effects and first-mover advantage'. They have 40 enterprise customers, and each customer's data is used only for that customer's model (illustrative).
drills.question: Which powers survive scrutiny, and which one could they actually build?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: No network effect: one customer's usage does not improve the product for another. No cross-customer data scale economy either, because data is siloed. First-mover advantage is not one of Helmer's powers. The realistic power is switching costs, through deep workflow integration and customer-specific models, plus possibly process power over time. The pitch should claim that, with evidence like retention and expansion.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Listing moat buzzwords without a benefit (higher price or lower cost) and a barrier that stops rivals copying it.

drills.title: Strategic acquisition or expensive habit
drills.scenario: Cisco closed its roughly $28B acquisition of Splunk in March 2024 at $157 a share (public record), adding a large observability and security software business.
drills.question: What three questions would you ask to judge whether a scope-expanding deal like this creates value?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: First, is there a real complementarity, meaning Splunk is worth more inside Cisco than alone (cross-sell to Cisco's installed base, data from network telemetry) by more than the premium paid? Second, can integration keep key talent and customers? Third, does the price leave a return above the cost of capital on realistic synergies? If value only exists in the synergy case, the deal rides on execution.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Justifying deals on strategic fit language while the premium already pays the target's shareholders for all the synergy.

drills.title: Find the bottleneck on the sandwich line
drills.scenario: A three-station sandwich line has capacities of 60, 40 and 120 sandwiches an hour. Demand is 40 an hour, giving utilizations of 67%, 100% and 33% (Foster OPMGT 502 class example, corrected math).
drills.question: Where would you add a worker, and what happens to throughput if you add one at station 3?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Station 2 is the bottleneck at 100% utilization; it sets throughput at 40 an hour. Adding capacity at station 3 adds zero throughput. Adding at station 2 helps only if demand rises above 40; today it mainly cuts queues and lead time. Run at 100% utilization, any variability makes the queue at station 2 grow.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Adding resources where people look busy or where it is easiest, instead of at the constraint.

drills.title: Little's Law for an LLM service
drills.scenario: An LLM inference service handles 50 requests a second. On average 400 requests are in the system at any moment (illustrative).
drills.question: What is the average latency, and what should you do if the target is 2 seconds?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Little's Law: lead time = WIP / throughput = 400 / 50 = 8 seconds, four times the target. To hit 2 seconds at 50 requests a second you need about 100 in system, so you must add serving capacity or cut service time (batching, smaller models, caching) so queues shrink. Also check utilization: near 100%, waiting time grows steeply.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Running GPUs at 95% utilization to look efficient, then being surprised by latency spikes.

drills.title: The A/B test that 'won'
drills.scenario: A product team ran 20 pricing-page variants for a week and reports one with a p-value of 0.04 and 6% higher conversion. They want to ship it (illustrative).
drills.question: Should they ship it?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Not on this evidence. With 20 variants at a 5% threshold, about one false positive is expected by chance. Correct for multiple comparisons, check the effect size and confidence interval, confirm the sample was planned rather than stopped early, then rerun the winner against control in a fresh test before shipping.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Testing many variants, peeking daily and shipping the first p < 0.05. That is how teams ship noise.

drills.title: Allocate scarce GPUs with a linear program
drills.scenario: A startup has 1,000 GPU-hours a week for two workloads: customer inference earning $30 margin per GPU-hour and model training valued at $20 per GPU-hour. Contracts require at least 300 GPU-hours of inference; training needs at least 200 to keep the roadmap on track (illustrative).
drills.question: Set up the allocation and state the answer and its shadow price.
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Maximize 30I + 20T subject to I + T <= 1,000, I >= 300, T >= 200. The optimum sets T at its minimum of 200 and I at 800, earning $28,000. The capacity constraint binds with a shadow price of $30 per extra GPU-hour, so renting more capacity pays if it costs under $30 an hour. The training floor costs $10 per hour versus putting that capacity into inference.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Splitting capacity by negotiation between teams instead of by marginal value, and never computing what an extra hour is worth.

drills.title: Dashboard says churn fell 40%
drills.scenario: After a data pipeline migration, the weekly dashboard shows churn down 40%. Nothing else in the business changed (illustrative).
drills.question: What do you check before telling the board?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Assume a data problem first. Check row counts before and after the migration, how 'active' and 'churned' are defined in the new SQL, duplicate or missing customer IDs from join changes, and time zone or late-arriving records. Reconcile churn to billing system cancellations. Only report it once two independent sources agree.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Celebrating a metric jump that coincides with a pipeline or definition change.

drills.title: Collaborate or compete with the incumbent
drills.scenario: A startup has a better AI model for reading medical scans. Hospitals buy through two dominant imaging equipment makers, who each have their own software roadmap (illustrative).
drills.question: Which strategy on the Entrepreneurial Strategy Compass fits, and why?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Likely collaborate and control the IP: license or partner through the equipment makers' channels instead of fighting them for distribution. The startup's edge is technology, while incumbents hold the customer relationships and regulatory complementary assets. Competing head-on means building sales, service and approvals from scratch. Protect the IP so the partner cannot simply copy it.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Defaulting to disrupt-the-incumbent because it is the story founders like, when the incumbent controls the scarce complementary assets.

drills.title: Which hypothesis do you test first?
drills.scenario: A founder planning a phone-camera vital-signs app lists hypotheses: users will pay $10 a month, the camera can read heart rate accurately on low-end phones, and clinics will recommend it (illustrative).
drills.question: Which do you test first, and with what kind of MVP?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Test the riskiest and cheapest-to-test assumption first. Accuracy on low-end phones is the hardest technical risk and blocks everything else, so build a crude prototype and benchmark it against a reference device on the target phones. Willingness to pay can be tested in parallel with a cheap landing page or pre-order, before any polished app.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Building the full product first, or testing the easy, flattering hypothesis while the fatal one sits untested.

drills.title: Price the robot on the farmer's payback
drills.scenario: Carbon Robotics' early seed pitch priced a laser weeding robot at about $120k including 3 years of service, with a bill of materials around $35k and roughly a 3-year payback for the farm (seed-pitch slide figures).
drills.question: Why price on customer ROI instead of cost-plus, and what is the gross margin?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Gross margin on hardware is about (120 - 35) / 120, roughly 71%, before service costs. Pricing on the farm's payback anchors the conversation on labor and herbicide savings, so a $120k price is easy to justify if the machine pays back in about 3 years. Cost-plus would have priced near $50k to $60k and left most of the value with the customer, starving the company of cash to fund R&D.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Engineer-founders pricing from their bill of materials instead of the customer's economics.

drills.title: The four beliefs behind a yes
drills.scenario: You have three minutes with a seed investor for a B2B AI startup. Your deck has 22 slides, mostly about the model architecture.
drills.question: What must the investor believe by the end, and how do you restructure the pitch?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: They must believe this team, this product, this market and this timing can produce a venture-scale outcome. Lead with a sharp problem and customer evidence, then why now, then the product in one demo, then the market and model, then the team's unfair advantage. Architecture goes in the appendix unless the technology itself is the moat.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Pitching the technology instead of the business. Investors buy outcomes, not architectures.

drills.title: The cash trough in the financial model
drills.scenario: A founder's model shows $1M ARR growing to $10M in three years, raising $5M now. Monthly burn peaks at $600k in month 18, and the model never shows cash going below zero (illustrative).
drills.question: What do you check, and how much should they raise?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Find the lowest point of the cumulative cash curve and check what drives it: hiring plan, sales cycle length and collections timing. Then stress it with a slower ramp and longer sales cycles. Raise enough to reach the next milestone plus a 6-month buffer under the stressed case, not the base case.
drills.antiPatternTrap: A model built top-down from ARR targets with no driver-based hiring or sales capacity, so the cash trough is fiction.

drills.title: Customer interviews that only confirm
drills.scenario: A founder ran 25 interviews. The summary says '23 out of 25 loved the idea and said they would use it.' No one has paid or signed a letter of intent (illustrative).
drills.question: What did the founder actually learn, and how should the next 10 interviews change?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Very little: compliments and hypothetical future use are weak evidence. Next interviews should ask about the last time the problem happened, what it cost, and what they already tried or paid for. End with a concrete ask, such as a pilot, a deposit or an introduction to the budget holder. Commitment, not enthusiasm, is the signal.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Pitching the solution in discovery interviews, which invites polite agreement.

drills.title: User, buyer and payer are three people
drills.scenario: A wellness screening app is loved by employees. Usage is high in a pilot at one company, but the deal stalls (illustrative).
drills.question: Map the ecosystem and say where the deal is stuck.
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: The user is the employee, the buyer is likely HR or benefits, and the payer may be the employer's benefits budget or an insurer. Usage proves user value but not buyer value. Build the case the buyer needs: participation, cost or risk reduction and an easy procurement and privacy review, and find who owns the budget.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Assuming user love closes enterprise deals. In B2B and healthcare, the person who pays often never uses the product.

drills.title: Is there product-market fit yet?
drills.scenario: An AI notes product has 5,000 signups. Week-4 retention is 12%. In a survey, 22% say they would be 'very disappointed' if the product went away (illustrative).
drills.question: Do they have product-market fit, and what is the next move?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Not yet. The common heuristic is about 40% 'very disappointed', and 12% retention with no flattening curve says users are not forming a habit. Segment the 22% who love it: find their job to be done, double down on that segment and cut features aimed at everyone else. Look for the retention curve to flatten before scaling acquisition.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Spending on growth before retention flattens, which pours users into a leaky bucket.

drills.title: Good-better-best for an AI product
drills.scenario: An AI meeting assistant charges $20 a seat with unlimited usage. Heavy users cost $15 a month in inference while light users cost $1 (illustrative).
drills.question: How would you restructure pricing?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Move to good-better-best tiers built on value metrics customers understand, for example a basic tier with a monthly usage allowance, a pro tier with more usage and advanced features, and an enterprise tier with admin, security and pooled usage. Add usage-based overage so heavy users pay closer to their cost. Anchor tiers on willingness to pay found through research, not on inference cost alone.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Flat unlimited pricing on a product with variable inference cost, which lets the heaviest users erase margin.

drills.title: Inference costs fall 50% a year
drills.scenario: An enterprise AI SaaS product has 55% gross margin today because of inference costs. Serving cost per request has been falling about 50% a year (illustrative).
drills.question: Should the company price for today's cost or tomorrow's, and what metric do you watch?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Price on customer value, not on either cost level, and let falling costs expand margin while keeping a buffer for competitors who cut price. Watch gross margin by cohort and CAC payback: if competitors pass savings to customers, prices fall too, so plan for value capture to shrink. Invest margin gains in differentiation that holds price.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Assuming falling costs automatically become profit. In competitive markets they often become lower prices.

drills.title: Positioning that tries to please everyone
drills.scenario: A startup describes its product as 'an AI platform for productivity, analytics and collaboration for teams of every size.' Win rates are low and sales cycles long (illustrative).
drills.question: Rewrite the positioning in one sentence using segmentation, targeting and positioning.
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Pick one beachhead segment where the product wins clearly, for example: 'For finance teams at mid-size SaaS companies who lose days to month-end close, we automate reconciliation in hours, unlike spreadsheets or generic BI tools.' Name the target, the pain, the outcome and the alternative. Expand to adjacent segments only after winning this one.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Broad positioning to avoid closing doors, which makes the product forgettable to everyone.

drills.title: The price change customers revolted against
drills.scenario: In 2011 Netflix split DVD and streaming into separately priced plans, about a 60% increase for customers who kept both, and announced a separate DVD brand, Qwikster. It lost roughly 800,000 subscribers in a quarter and dropped Qwikster within weeks (public record).
drills.question: What went wrong in the marketing, not just the price?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: The strategy of shifting to streaming was arguably right, but the execution broke trust: a large price jump with little notice, no added value framed for customers, and a brand split that made life harder. Better: grandfather or phase pricing, lead with what customers gain, and test reactions in segments before a full rollout.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Treating pricing as a finance decision and announcing it without customer framing or a migration path.

drills.title: Community-led growth after an acquisition
drills.scenario: Microsoft bought Mojang, maker of Minecraft, in 2014 for $2.5B (public record). Minecraft's growth had been driven by its player and creator community rather than paid marketing.
drills.question: As the acquirer's marketing lead, what do you protect and what do you change?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Protect the community's trust: keep the product's character, creator tools and cross-platform play, and avoid monetization that feels like a cash grab. Change what scale can improve, such as education programs, new platforms and licensed merchandise. Measure community health (creator activity, engagement) alongside revenue.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Applying the parent's standard monetization playbook to a community-built brand and losing the engine that made it valuable.

drills.title: Star engineer, struggling first-time manager
drills.scenario: Your best engineer was promoted to lead a team of six. Three months in, they still write most of the critical code, reviews are bottlenecked on them, and two people have asked to transfer (illustrative).
drills.question: What do you tell them in your next one-on-one?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Name the shift: their output is now the team's output, not their own code. Agree to hand off critical code paths with pairing, delegate review authority, and set up weekly one-on-ones with each report. Give them a concrete measure, like team throughput and retention, and coach them on it monthly. Offer a senior IC track if they prefer to stay technical.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Promoting the best individual contributor and assuming the skills transfer, then judging them on their personal output.

drills.title: Founder succession at scale
drills.scenario: Disney's board brought Bob Iger back as CEO in November 2022, replacing his hand-picked successor Bob Chapek after less than three years (public record).
drills.question: What does a board owe the company on CEO succession, and what failed here?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: A board should run succession as a continuous process: several internal and external candidates developed over years, clear criteria tied to strategy, and real overlap so the board judges the successor directly, not through the outgoing CEO. Signs of failure here include a narrow candidate slate, a rushed handover and a reversal that signaled no ready alternative.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Delegating succession to the incumbent CEO and treating it as a one-time event.

drills.title: Tell the board the quarter missed
drills.scenario: Your startup missed its quarterly revenue plan by 25% because two large deals slipped. The board meeting is tomorrow and you have five minutes on the agenda (illustrative).
drills.question: Structure the five minutes.
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Lead with the bottom line in one sentence: the miss, its size and the cause. Then show what is in your control (pipeline health, slipped deal status, cash runway impact) and the plan with dates. Close with the specific help or decision you need from the board. Send the numbers in advance so the meeting is for discussion, not discovery.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Burying bad news at the end, or surprising the board in the meeting instead of calling the chair beforehand.

drills.title: Recall now or wait for proof
drills.scenario: In 1982 Johnson & Johnson pulled about 31 million bottles of Tylenol nationwide after seven deaths in the Chicago area from capsules tampered with after they left the factory (public record).
drills.question: Why was the costly recall the right call, and how would you apply it to an AI product safety issue?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: J&J put customer safety first, acted before having full proof, communicated openly and redesigned packaging, which helped rebuild trust and market share. For an AI product: if a model is causing harm, pause or limit the feature quickly, disclose what you know, fix root causes and explain the safeguards. Delay to protect revenue usually costs more trust later.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Waiting for certainty or legal sign-off while harm continues, then managing it as a PR problem.

drills.title: Incentives that manufactured fraud
drills.scenario: In 2016 Wells Fargo was fined $185M after employees opened roughly 2 million unauthorized accounts to meet aggressive cross-selling targets; later reviews raised the count to about 3.5 million (public record).
drills.question: Where did leadership fail, and what would you design differently in a sales or growth team?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Leaders set targets that could not be met honestly, rewarded volume over customer value, and fired low-level employees instead of fixing the system. Design differently: tie incentives to customer outcomes and quality (retention, complaints), audit for gaming, protect whistleblowers, and hold senior leaders accountable for the system.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Treating misconduct as a few bad actors when the incentive system made it predictable.

drills.title: A board without the expertise to ask
drills.scenario: Theranos had a board of famous former officials and executives but almost no members with laboratory science or medical device expertise, while the company claimed it could run many tests from a finger-prick of blood (public record).
drills.question: What board composition and processes would have caught the problem?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Add directors with relevant technical and regulatory expertise, plus an independent audit or science committee with authority to commission outside validation. Require independent evidence for core claims, direct access to staff and auditors, and executive sessions without the CEO. Prestige is not oversight; the board must be able to test the central claim.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Choosing directors for status and network, leaving no one able to challenge the founder on the core technology.

drills.title: Dual-class control and the IPO that collapsed
drills.scenario: WeWork pulled its 2019 IPO after investors scrutinized its filing: super-voting founder shares, payments to the founder for the 'We' trademark, leases on buildings he had stakes in, and a private valuation that had reached $47B (public record).
drills.question: Which governance red flags would you raise as an independent director, and what fixes would you insist on before listing?
drills.cfoFounderAnswer: Red flags: concentrated voting control with no sunset, related-party transactions, a board unable to remove or check the CEO, and a valuation unsupported by unit economics. Fixes: a time-based sunset on super-voting shares, unwinding related-party deals, an independent chair or lead director, and a financial story that holds up on public-market metrics.
drills.antiPatternTrap: Accepting founder control terms because the last private round did, assuming public investors will too.
